Rajni: Thanks. You lost by seven votes, Sarita. I keep thinking about it.
Sarita: I did. And it stings, I won't pretend. Can I ask you something? What did you do that I didn't?

passage:
Last September I lost the school captain election to Parul by six votes. Six. I remember standing near the notice board, face burning, pretending to read a sports fixture.

I wanted to disappear for a week. Instead, before lunch, I walked to Parul's class and shook her hand. She looked surprised, then said, "Thanks. Your canteen idea was good, you know."

That stuck with me. So I asked two teachers what I could have done better. One said my speech was all problems and no small first steps. Fair.

Then I went to Parul again and offered to run a canteen committee under her. She agreed. Now four of us meet every Friday, and last month the canteen finally started a second billing counter.

I'm Jatin. I'm not captain, but the thing I campaigned for happened anyway.

qa.q: By how many votes did Jatin lose?
How did Jatin feel standing near the notice board after the result?
qa.a: Jatin felt humiliated and crushed, face burning and wanting to disappear for a week.

qa.q: What else could Jatin do to keep learning from this loss?
qa.a: Jatin could note the teachers' feedback and draft small first steps for any future plan, so the next campaign shows how, not just what.

qa.q: How might Parul see Jatin's offer to run the canteen committee?
qa.a: Parul probably felt relieved and glad, because a rival became a helper and her team gained someone who cared about the canteen.

grounding: A reflective account of a student who loses narrowly, congratulates the winner, asks for feedback and leads a committee to do the promised work anyway.

Note from the social science teacher, for the student council file

On the day results were announced, Kishore lost the school captain election to Lakshmi by eleven votes. I was watching the hall because I expected tears or anger. There were neither, at least not in public.

He waited until the crowd thinned, walked up to Lakshmi and congratulated her. That afternoon he came to the staffroom and asked me, quite formally, what he could have done differently. I told him his speech had many ideas but no plan for any of them.

Two days later he brought me a written proposal for a library committee, the main issue he had campaigned on, and asked whether Lakshmi would accept him as its lead. She did. I have approved the committee and will check its first report next month.

qa.q: What did Kishore bring to the teacher two days later?
qa.a: He brought a written proposal for a library committee.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling when he waited for the crowd to thin?
qa.a: He may have felt disappointed and hurt but wanted to stay composed, choosing a quieter moment to congratulate Lakshmi.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next to support the committee?
qa.a: The teacher could help Kishore set one small goal for the first month, so the committee's report shows a real result.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see Kishore's request to lead the library committee?
qa.a: Lakshmi may feel respected and relieved, since the rival accepted the result and offered to work under the council.

grounding: A teacher's note records a student who lost by a few votes, congratulated the winner, asked for feedback and offered to lead a committee on his issue.
